svg.title: A cauldron is a large cooking pot: the central object in the witches’ chant.

text.tspan: A cauldron is a large cooking pot: the central object in the witches’ chant.
Double, double toil and trouble;
Fire burn, and cauldron bubble.
William Shakespeare · Macbeth, Act IV, Scene 1 (First Folio) · Published 1623
A rhythmic chant that creates a supernatural atmosphere
in a scene from Macbeth.
a spell-like chant; a rhythmic incantation · These describe
the kind of speech; they are not substitute quotations.
During rehearsal, the actors stressed “Double, double”
and the repeated b sounds to give the witches’ chant its
driving rhythm.
Macbeth, Act 4, Scene 1; first published in the First Folio
(1623). The speakers are the witches, not Shakespeare
speaking personally. Toil means hard work; a cauldron is a
large pot.
A: Shall I whisper the whole line to make it sound sinister?
B: Try stressing “Double, double” first. The repetition gives
it a pulse.
A: And make “burn” and “bubble” sharper?
B: Exactly. Let the sounds create the tension rather than
simply making your voice louder.
You are directing this line for a school performance.
Identify one repetition and one repeated consonant sound.
Explain how you would use them in delivery.
